text:
EA Sports FC 27 Review
EA Sports FC 27 reviewed by Andrew McMahon on PS5 Pro, also available on PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC.

"EA Sports FC 27 is a game caught between two competing directions. The revamped passing and crossing, deeper Career Mode systems, and greater emphasis on strategy give more meaningful control and reflect the improvements that help build on the series’ strongest foundations. At the same time, those improvements are repeatedly undermined by inconsistent CPU behavior, lingering defensive issues, technical problems, slow menus, and an open-world hub that is disconnected from what fans want from a virtual soccer experience. So while the soccer itself is enjoyable, the series is still searching for the right balance between innovation and making the core game work the way it should."

text:
Bungie Says Marathon Flopped Because It Was Too Hard - IGN Daily Fix
In today's Daily Fix:
Bungie thinks they may have figured out what went wrong with Marathon, and it just might be too damn hard. Marathon's senior design lead, Kevin Yanes, admits that the "constant loop failure" didn't resonate with players in the way Bungie had hoped. Marathon has been hemorraging players since its debut earlier in the year, which may have lead Bungie to revive Destiny 2 content. In other news, The Verge has revealed the next Halo Studios-made Halo game was still years away, forcing Microsoft to pull the project and hand the IP over to Activision. It's been five years since Halo Infinite, which itself was five years after Halo 5. And finally, Insider Gaming reports that Ubisoft pitched a Zelda game to Nintendo...with Gannondorf as the protagonist. Nintendo decided not to pursue the project after seeing a prototype in 2023.

text:
How One Crash Bandicoot Level Helped Build Naughty Dog | Art of the Level
There are hundreds of cinematic chase sequences in video games and they can all trace their roots back to an unlikely source. The colourful cartoon platformer that started it all: Crash Bandicoot.

The running-towards-camera chase sequence is as popular now as it’s ever been, raising the cinematic tension in blockbuster games for the last 30 years. But its beginnings were humble, and its widespread use is all thanks to the Crash developers at Naughty Dog trying to solve a single problem: How do we show our Crash Bandicoot’s face more?

From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design.
